title: Iterative Policy Optimization: Batch-Online Multi-Turn RL via Single-Turn RL
claim: Multi-turn RL reduces to alternating single-turn reward-model fitting and single-turn policy optimization, with future turns compressed into a learned Q-function.
layout: 3 regions, top-down with feedback loop; funnel graphic shows compressed future turns
description: The figure has two stacked gray rounded panels and a feedback loop. The top panel, "Learn multi-turn Q^π", shows an orange Q^π-model box with a neural-net icon. Dotted arrows connect it to three episode bars made of gray token squares. The bars are split into turns by dashed lines and end in +0 or +1 rewards, with turn labels underneath. The bottom-left panel, "Single-turn GRPO", shows a blue LLM box with a net icon. It sends a single-turn response of tokens to an orange Q^π box, which returns an estimated multi-turn return in a loop. To the right, an orange funnel fans out from Q^π into faded, branching future-turn token sequences. These illustrate turns that are compressed rather than generated. A blue LLM π′ (improved) box at the bottom feeds back to the top through a dotted "Repeat π ← π′" arrow. Orange marks Q^π and blue marks the LLM.
caption: Reducing multi-turn to single-turn RLHF via IterPO. We visualize the main steps of our proposed approach. At the top, we collect multi-turn trajectories under the current policy $\pi$, compute Monte Carlo returns, and use standard reward-modeling procedures to fit the turn-level $Q$-function $Q^\pi$, which predicts the expected total multi-turn reward under $\pi$. At the bottom, holding $Q^\pi$ fixed, we run standard single-turn (token-level) GRPO using $Q^\pi$ as the reward model. Future conversation turns are implicitly "compressed" into $Q^\pi$, allowing candidate responses to be scored without simulator rollouts during policy improvement. The right side shows how iterating this procedure ($\pi \leftarrow \pi'$) yields multi-turn improvements using only single-turn RLHF tools. Since we proceed in a series of deployment rounds, we refer to this as "batch-online."
abstract: Practical LLM agents often operate over multi-turn conversations where success is determined only after the full interaction ends. Most multi-turn RL methods train via on-policy rollouts, but unlike in single-turn RL, the policy cannot produce a trajectory alone, since an external environment must respond after each agent turn. For conversational agents, this environment is a user, but real users are generally unavailable inside the training loop and simulated users are difficult to build faithfully. Separately, real-world deployment is rarely fully online or fully offline. The common production pattern is called batch online, where the current policy is deployed to collect a batch of interaction data, then retrained on that batch and redeployed. We show that this batch-online setting creates an opportunity for applying the classical approximate policy iteration algorithm. Our central observation is that running standard token-level, single-turn GRPO with a learned turn-level $Q$-function as the reward model is a policy improvement step for the multi-turn problem. Building on this, we present Iterative Policy Optimization (IterPO), which alternates between fitting $Q^Ï$ from logged Monte Carlo returns via standard reward modeling (policy evaluation) and running single-turn GRPO against $Q^Ï$ (policy improvement). During policy improvement, the learned $Q^Ï$ scores candidate responses by their expected downstream return, avoiding the need for simulator rollouts of the remaining conversation. Overall, this allows us to do principled multi-turn RL using only single-turn RL methods without an interactive environment or user simulator inside the training loop. We demonstrate the effectiveness of IterPO on six multi-turn negotiation environments.
